title: Self Induction (Inertia of Electricity) and Self Inductance

claims.text: Self induction, also called inertia of electricity: when a coil connected to a battery is switched on, current takes time to rise from 0 to its saturation/maximum value (rather than jumping instantly); during this rise the changing current produces a changing magnetic field and hence changing flux through the coil itself, which (by Lenz's law) induces a back EMF opposing the current's growth. Similarly, at switch-off, as current falls from maximum to 0, the coil again opposes this change (now opposing the decrease), so current takes some time to die out. This resistance to any CHANGE in its own current (much like mechanical inertia resists change in a body's velocity) is why self-induction is called the inertia of electricity

Definition: self-induction is the property of a coil by virtue of which it opposes the growth or decay of current flowing through it. The EMF induced in the coil itself (due to its own changing current) is called the back EMF

Conceptual example: a battery and key connect to two parallel branches -- one with an inductor L in series with bulb B1, the other with a resistor R in series with bulb B2. Question 1: which bulb glows immediately when the key is closed? Since the inductor opposes the growth of current (while an ideal resistor does not oppose current growth at all), maximum current initially flows through the resistor branch, so B2 glows immediately (B1 lights up gradually as current in the inductor branch builds up). Question 2: after both bulbs have been glowing steadily and the key is switched off, which bulb glows for longer? Since the inductor opposes the DECREASE in current (while the resistor does not), B1 (the inductor branch) continues to glow for longer after switch-off

Why sparks occur when switching household circuits on/off: switching on causes voltage to jump rapidly (e.g. 0 to 230 V), so flux changes very rapidly, inducing a very large EMF; this large EMF is enough to ionize the air gap at the switch contacts, making it briefly conducting -- producing a spark. The same happens at switch-off as current rapidly falls from its maximum to zero. This is why circuits should never be switched on or off if there is a gas leak in the vicinity (the spark could be fatal). Modern switches include a small resistor between the contacts so that current can pass through it during switching, reducing the rate of change and hence reducing sparking

Non-inductive winding of household AC wires: since AC current is continuously changing, ordinary coiled wire would produce significant self-induction. To minimize this, household copper wires are twisted together (wound back and forth on themselves) so that the current in adjacent, opposite-direction sections is equal and opposite; the magnetic fields from these opposite currents cancel each other out, giving minimum self-induction. Such wiring is called a non-inductive coil

Coefficient of self-induction (self-inductance) L: the magnetic flux linked with a coil is proportional to the current flowing through it, phi proportional to i. Introducing a constant of proportionality, phi = Li, where L is called the coefficient of self-induction or self-inductance. Setting i=1 ampere gives L=phi, so ONE DEFINITION of L is: the magnetic flux linked with the coil when unit current flows through it
A second definition of L, via EMF: starting from e=-dphi/dt and substituting phi=Li, e=-d(Li)/dt=-L(di/dt). This equation (e=-L di/dt) is very important and used in many numericals

A third phrasing of the definition, directly from e=-L(di/dt): if the rate of change of current (di/dt) is unity (1 A/s), then L=e -- i.e. the coefficient of self-induction equals the EMF induced when the current changes at unit rate. Units of L: from L=phi/I, units are Wb/A, also called the HENRY (H); from L=e/(di/dt), units are V.A^-1.s. 1 H = 1 V.A^-1.s = 1 Wb.A^-1. Dimensional formula of L: [M L^2 T^-2 A^-2]

markdown_body:
## Self induction: inertia of electricity (NCERT 6.7)

When a coil is switched on, current takes time to rise to its maximum value rather than jumping instantly: the changing current produces changing flux through the coil itself, inducing a **back EMF** (by Lenz's law) that opposes the current's growth. At switch-off, the coil similarly opposes the current's decay. This resistance to *any change* in its own current — analogous to mechanical inertia — is why self-induction is called the **inertia of electricity**.

**Definition:** self-induction is the property of a coil by virtue of which it opposes the growth or decay of current flowing through it.

### Conceptual example
Battery + key feed two parallel branches: inductor $L$ + bulb $B_1$, and resistor $R$ + bulb $B_2$.
- **On switch-close:** $L$ opposes current growth, $R$ doesn't $\Rightarrow$ $B_2$ glows **immediately**; $B_1$ brightens gradually.
- **On switch-open** (after both are steady): $L$ opposes the current's decrease $\Rightarrow$ $B_1$ glows **for longer**.

### Sparking and non-inductive winding
Rapid voltage change at switching ($0\to230$ V or back) induces a large EMF, ionizing the air gap at switch contacts $\Rightarrow$ a spark (why circuits should never be switched near a gas leak). Modern switches add a small resistor between contacts to reduce this. Household AC wires are **twisted** together so current in adjacent opposite-direction sections is equal and opposite, cancelling the magnetic field — a **non-inductive coil**, minimizing self-induction.

## Self-inductance $L$

Flux linked with a coil is proportional to current: $\phi \propto i \Rightarrow \phi = Li$, where $L$ is the **coefficient of self-induction** (self-inductance).

**Three equivalent definitions:**
1. Setting $i=1$ A: $L=\phi$ — flux linked with the coil per unit current.
2. From $e=-d\phi/dt = -d(Li)/dt$: $\boxed{e = -L\dfrac{di}{dt}}$
3. Setting $di/dt=1$ A/s: $L=e$ — the EMF induced per unit rate of change of current.

**Units:** $L=\phi/I \Rightarrow$ Wb/A $=$ **Henry (H)**; also $L=e/(di/dt)\Rightarrow$ V$\cdot$A$^{-1}\cdot$s. $1\text{ H} = 1\text{ V}\cdot\text{A}^{-1}\cdot\text{s} = 1\text{ Wb}\cdot\text{A}^{-1}$.
**Dimensional formula:** $[L] = [ML^2T^{-2}A^{-2}]$
